name: Thailand
snapshot: Anutin Charnvirakul rode nationalist anger over the border war with Cambodia to a landslide in a snap election in early 2026.
culture: Thailand was never colonised, and the monarchy is revered and protected by strict lese-majeste laws. Buddhism shapes daily life, and most young men spend time as monks. Thai food, Muay Thai boxing and Songkran, the April water festival, are global exports. Thai TV dramas and "boys' love" series have big audiences across Asia.
society: Thailand is a manufacturing and tourism powerhouse, but growth has been sluggish and household debt is high. Since 2006, the army and courts have repeatedly removed elected governments, many linked to Thaksin Shinawatra. Insurgents in the Muslim-majority far south have fought the state for two decades.
situation: For 20 years Thai politics has been a fight between the conservative establishment of army, palace and courts and the parties of Thaksin Shinawatra and, later, young reformers. The establishment usually lost elections and won anyway, by coup or court ruling. In 2026, for the first time in decades, a party of the establishment simply won.

Anutin Charnvirakul, who became prime minister in September 2025 after a court removed Thaksin's daughter Paetongtarn over a leaked phone call with Cambodia's Hun Sen, called a snap election during the border war with Cambodia. On 8 February his Bhumjaithai party, known before mainly for legalising cannabis, won 192 of 500 seats, up from 71 (Reuters via NST). The progressive People's Party, which had led every poll, fell to about 117, and Thaksin's Pheu Thai had its worst result ever (Malay Mail). Analysts credited nationalism over the Cambodia clashes, defections of rural MPs to Bhumjaithai, and the People's Party's damaging decision to prop Anutin up in office in 2025 (Asialink). Anutin formed a coalition with Pheu Thai and was re-elected prime minister on 19 March. The young urban voters who powered the reformist wave of 2023 are now in opposition, and the promised rewrite of the military-era constitution looks less urgent to those in power.
power: A constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system. The prime minister needs a majority in the 500-seat House of Representatives; the king is revered and protected by strict lèse-majesté laws, and the courts and military have repeatedly removed elected governments.
holders: Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul (Bhumjaithai), re-elected March 2026; King Vajiralongkorn.
